The main cause of all ocean currents is wind; and if there were no atmosphere there would be no Gulf Stream or any other similar movement of the sea. The entire surface of the Atlantic north of the region of the trade winds is driven towards the north-east by the prevailing drift of the air. Its movements are the direct result of the atmospheric circulation in the great cyclonic system which rests over the North Atlantic with its centre at Iceland. Not only is wind the effective agent in the oceanic circulation which brings us water from lower latitudes, but to it also must be mainly ascribed the relatively high winter temperature, as well as the comparative freedom from extremes of heat and cold, which distinguish the climate of the British Isles and other parts of Western Europe. The prevailing winds are south-west and west, and they reach our islands charged with moisture, much of which is deposited as rain. This means the release of vast quantities of latent heat, which accounts, therefore, for the mildness of the west coasts in comparison with the east. Without our warm and moist winds blowing from the Atlantic the British climate would be rigorously cold.

THE Gulf Stream is really only an incidental part of the general surface circulation of the North Atlantic, by virtue of which there is a steady drift of ocean water in a north-easterly direction. If the Gulf Stream did not exist, the coasts of western and north-western Europe would still be in the line of this drift current of relatively warm water from lower latitudes. As the stream loses itself near Newfoundland, oceanographers now usually term the current off western Europe the Atlantic Current or European Current. Moreover, there is undoubted evidence that warm salt water from the Mediterranean extends even beyond the North Cape of Norway, and it is this rather than water which has passed through the Gulf of Mexico which probably explains why no icebergs appear off the coast of Europe.

At no place around our coasts is the average annual temperature of the sea more than two degrees above that of the air; and the differences between sea and air temperatures are usually much over-estimated, especially on the western coast. The Gulf Stream has been given credit which belongs to the whole mass of the Atlantic, and ocean water that which belongs to wind. The driving force of atmospheric circulation is the sun, and we must look, therefore, chiefly to variations of solar heat for the cause of differences in this circulation year by year. It has been shown by Drs. Holland-Hansen and Nansen that variations in the temperature of the Atlantic Current from one year to another are followed by corresponding variations in the winter climate of Norway and also by variations in the fisheries of the North Sea. Some observations made in connection with the Marine Biological Laboratory at Lowestoft, referred to in the Daily Mail, confirm this relationship. Variations of air temperature in the North Atlantic, however, precede, and are not the result of, the temperature of the water, so that from whatever point of view the subject of our climate and its changes is surveyed the conclusion is reached that the determining influence is not water but wind; or, alternatively, in legal phrase, if it is water, then it is not the Gulf Stream, which disappears in the Atlantic a couple of thousand miles to the west of these islands.

ILLUSTRATIONS of heroic recoveries, the result of patience and faith, are not uncommon. There came before one of the Metropolitan police courts recently a man charged with malicious damage to property. This offence took the form of breaking windows always within sight of a police officer. The impulse was neither drink nor unemployment, neither was it politics nor lunacy. He was protesting against nothing, and he had a grievance against nobody, yet the offence recurred. The offender had served several terms of imprisonment, and on the days of his discharge from prison he repeated his offences. His attitude in the dock was one of silence and indifference, save for his monosyllabic "yes" when asked to plead.

There is in an obscure byway of London a man who has recovered the will to live and labour, and if anybody wants cabinet work into which is wrought something of his rediscovered joy, he can have it, and in it the tangible expression of the worth of trying to understand the heart of a man who has nearly lost his way.

WHILST the Law is technical and inelastic and emphatic in its requirements to prove a prisoner guilty, it is elastic, adaptable and generous in favour of a prisoner. Technicalities and, indeed, express provisions, are looked at lightly when justice and mercy can meet together. Sometimes grave charges are reduced to charges less grave, and offences that strictly should be treated as indictable and sent for trial to the Central Criminal Court are dealt with summarily.

EVERY attempt made to get at some understanding of his motive was met with "I've nothing to say, sir," and he said nothing, in spite of every wile and inducement. Here was a man standing in splendid isolation to life. He had no interest in and no concern for the affairs that appeal to the ordinary citizen. Time after time he threw himself into the stream that washed him into the solitude of his prison retreat. He chose a way of crime that involved little or no social stigma, and he did the wrong that impinged least on the moral law. The psychology was simple enough. The prisoner, for some reason or another, had lost the will to hold his place amongst men; he had got "out of step" with the world and had no desire to regain it. The normal operation of law punishment had no relativity to such a case as this. Here was needed some warm human trial without cant and without officialism. This was tried. The prisoner was brought into a little sitting-room, treated like a visitor and spoken to as man to man. There was no motive in his behaviour that the most cynical could suspect. He was as onished, but recalcitrant.

There appeared at a Metropolitan police court a man charged with a series of offences running from drunk and disorderly to malicious damage to property and assaults on the police. The cause causans was drink, the cause the insults and taunts of a female neighbour. Under the influence of drink he replied to the taunts by an attack on the woman's possessions, and in his passion he assaulted the police officers who tried to restrain him. A night in the cells had stillled the raging tempest, and in the morning the prisoner's view of the occurrence was almost judicial. Alas ! Repentance does not bring forgiveness in human affairs, and men must pay the price of folly. He had learnt that.

He pleaded guilty, and then the thing that he dreaded happened—the resurrection of his past. There were stories of violence before—violence that had ben atomed for in penal servitude. One watched, and one pitied him for the anguish of his suffering. An outburst of passion, and all the present is alive with the things that he had thought to be dead! Purgatory can be created and men can suffer an-eternity of anguish in a moment. But the police had more to say. The last sentence was a dozen years ago, and the intervening years were years of industry and honesty and effort to retrieve the past. The police laid stress on this outburst as a momentary lapse in a hard fight. Of repentance and regret there could be no doubt. They were written in the deepened lines on the grey face that had missed its sleep. "A past," sometimes is the superlative justification for generosity, and surely this was such a case. The speedier the justice the more just it would be. To hold in suspense a man who had waged a good warfare since his last release seemed unjustifiable and cruel. One felt this experience was all that was needed to establish him in his path of righteousness, and justice could ordain only one decree, namely, to send him back to freedom, with a warning against drink and the tongues of women. (To be continued.)

The prisoner repeated his brief litany, "I've nothing to say, sir," but his eyes spoke when his lips were silent. He was remanded for a week, when there was another little talk and he was given another chance. The court intermediary set him up in his trade, in a little workshop and undertook to find a market for his "creations."

In the administration of the Criminal Law it is seldom that much difficulty arises in deciding whether a man is guilty or not guilty, or whether he should be committed for trial or discharged. Stipendiary magistrates have had experience in criminal courts and learnt at the Bar the principles of the Law and the application of those principles. Even in the higher courts which try indictable offences, when the jury have discharged their function of finding a prisoner guilty, the real difficulty begins after that finding of fact. What is to be done with him? The law gives a very wide discretion in the matter of punishment to judges and magistrates. It is a great trust, on which infinite possibilities depend. Shall the prisoner be given a chance and bound over to come up for judgment if called upon? Shall he be punished by fine or imprisonment or penal servitude? If so, in what amount, or for what term? The prisoner's past is open. It may be a story of industry and honesty, or it may be a record of crime. A clean record may only mean that the prisoner has been lucky in his escape up till now, or it may mean he has succumbed to a sudden temptation by reason of his circumstances. A black record may mean that the prisoner is definitely and deliberately pursuing a career of crime, or it may mean that he has been fighting a good fight to regain his lost reputation and been stricken in the midst of his warfare.
